utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Jordash, you wished to raise a preliminary matter, if I'm well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you, Your Honours. Yesterday at the close of the court day we had an exchange about the information which had been communicated from the UNDU medical service to the court and to myself, and I think I spoke rather hastily because the conversation made me go back to the questions that were put to the doctor and the answers that we received, and it's my fault for not studying the questions or the answers in more detail once I received them. But having done that, I am concerned, and for this reason: Your Honours will remember the questions filed on the 7th of December, 2011, and one of those questions was, and I look at question 3: "What treatment including psychiatric or psychological therapy does Mr. Stanisic receive at the UNDU as opposed to the specialist treatment received as an outpatient in Dutch hospitals?" And what evoked that question from the Stanisic Defence was a request to the Registry for Mr. Stanisic's medical records and the first batch that arrived only contained medical records relating to his treatment at specialist hospitals. We've since received a second batch but as yet they have not been translated, so I couldn't look at them in depth. But in relation to that question, the answer we received on the 9th of December, 2011, was: "Mr. Stanisic is treated with medication he needs for his medical problems. When new complaints occur, these will then be examined." And it's that answer which concerns me. And it concerns me because it doesn't really say anything other than what we know, is that he receives medication for his medical problems. But it concerns me because I still, having tried to get an answer to this question on several occasions, don't know the answer to this essential question, what happens with Mr. Stanisic in the UNDU in terms of treatment. Does he receive psychological therapy? Does he receive psychiatric therapy? Does he receive medication as a regular thing, or does he just see the doctor, have a chat, or whatever? I just don't know. And I haven't known, I don't think, for the last two and a half years, and it's that which I would like to know so I can discuss that with Mr. Stanisic, and he's instructed me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider how to improve the communication and we'll consider how to do that that might, I'm very cautious, be that the Chamber further inquires with the Registry, but I do agree that if you ask for whether he receives psychological, psychiatric treatment than to say he receives whatever he needs is not a real answer. I tend to agree with that. At the same time, of course, one wonders whether Mr. Stanisic himself could tell you whether he receives any psychological or psychiatric treatment. I mean, if he -- I don't know how often he, and whether he, sees a psychiatrist. So as a patient myself, I have at least some idea on what kind of treatment I receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So to that extent it's communication, I would say, because if you say I would like to hear what treatment he receives so that I can discuss it with him, I would first of all, of course, ask him what kind of medication he receives and whether it's prescribed by the specialist or whether in addition to that other medication is prescribed by the treating medical officer at the UNDU. But it's of no use to start discussing this here at this moment. It clearly is a matter which causes again and again problems and where the smooth communications seems not to have been achieved yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's -- I mean, I have, and I've repeatedly said this to the Registry - and I say it now - that I'm not on behalf of Mr. Stanisic making any complaint other than it's we would like some information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes [Overlapping speakers]. If you ask what treatment does he receives and the answer is he receives the treatment he needs, is not very elucidating the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Any other matter? Now, since we are -- I don't think as a matter of fact that we have received this morning, let me just check. I have nothing as far as waiver is concerned because Mr. Stanisic, and we should put that on the record, is absent, not surprising in view of the information received yesterday, but do you have any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is at this very moment that Madam Registrar informs me that the waiver has -- a copy of the waiver has arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I haven't as yet seen that. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'll just put it on the record. I just received a copy of an ... of an absence-from-court-due-to-illness form. First one signed by Mr. Stanisic, I take it. It's not very clear but it -- the box is ticked which says, "I'm unable to attend court proceeding on this date due to illness." The second one has been ticked as well, "I have discussed the with my counsel." That must then refer to an earlier discussion, I take it. And then the third box is, "I understand that I have a right to be present at all trial proceedings against me; however, I waive my right to be present in court on this date and give my consent for the proceedings to continue in my absence but in the presence of my counsel." The second box ticked is a bit of a surprise, that he has discussed it with counsel, but again --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, he's discussed -- I think he's discussed it yesterday with Mr. Martin, and today when Mr. Martin called, he was in the UNDU hospital, but I suspect Mr. Stanisic is referring to the conversation yesterday which made it quite clear that he was happy for this witness to be heard in his absence if he couldn't make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The principal officer says that he confirms receipt of this -- receipt of this form from the detainee named over at 7.20, I take it that's 7.20 a.m., and there is a date and a signature there, the date the 14th of December. Now, the usual form with the UNDU medical service questions, that is the one usually filled in by the nurse, is empty which can be explained by the fact that Mr. Stanisic may not be at the UNDU itself at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, having looked at this, would you like to have a -- would you like to have a look at it too?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm happy for us to go on while that's being done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll proceed and at the same time a copy may be given to Mr. Jordash. Yes. Thank you. Then any other preliminary matter? Then I would like to read the decision which I had on my mind to read yesterday, but I'd first like to inquire whether the booth have received copies? It is a decision on the Republic of Serbia request for extension of time to file submissions in relation to protective measures for four witnesses. On the 23rd of November, 2011, the Chamber requested that Serbia be provided with the portions provisionally held in private session of the transcripts of the witnesses Novakovic, Corbic, Dragicevic, and Lekovic. The Chamber invited Serbia to file reasoned submissions within two weeks of the receipt of the transcripts, identifying which portions should remain confidential. On the 13th of December, 2011, Serbia requested additional time to file its submissions. The Chamber grants Serbia an extension of four weeks from the date of this decision, that is the 14th of December, to file its submissions. The Chamber encourages Serbia to prepare its submissions and any possible future requests for protective measures in accordance with the Chamber's decisions of the 3rd of November and the 2nd of October -- I have to correct myself. The decision of the 3rd of November, 2009, and the 7th of October, 2011, and the reasons of the 23rd of November, 2011. That may reduce the need for the filing of further submissions following testimony in relation to possible future requests. The Chamber instructs the Registry to provide Serbia with the transcript of this oral decision. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Then I think there are no further obstacles to continue the cross-examination of the witness. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Has there been any further communication between Prosecution and Defence yesterday about the chart?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There has, Your Honour. However, it's tentative. I think what the plan is, is to sit down immediately after or shortly after today's session, go through the chart. There has been some discussion as to what may be acceptable to include and what our concerns would be, so the Prosecution look forward -- looks forward to discussing this further with the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, same optimistic feeling?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We discussed that, I have no problem with that. Even if Mr. Weber were to wait for the translations of the redacted portions so that he would have a complete picture with regard to these documents, then we could have this meeting because we asked to have the redacted portions translated too and then we are going to have a complete picture and discuss all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the problems is that the witness might have left by the time you -- you are finishing your -- concluding your discussions. Mr. Lucic, it's very impolite to continue talking on other matters when you enter the courtroom. Good morning to you and apologies. I would like to remind you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday, that is that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jordash will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning. I just want to pick up where we left off yesterday, and I'll remind you what you said yesterday which was, to Your Honours, page 88 of the draft transcript: "He, Dragan, was scaring the army with the DB in order to make them do what he wanted them to do because he knew that there was always an antagonism there." Now, I'm not going to suggest any answer to you. I want you to tell us what precisely you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in Tito's period, this antagonism was created between the army and the police. Perhaps we can say that it was like a clash between two clans for the love of Tito. That is how Tito tried to prevent any one of the services betraying him. The military intelligence service and the State Security Service, perhaps we can put it that way, were hostile to each other as they served the regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did that hostility continue or change after Tito's death, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not change. It had become a mannerism, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How do you say that Dragan used that antagonism?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a stick. He threatened the army that he would seek support from the other force within the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you speak to him about this?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not speak about it at the time. I did later because he was disappointed by the general situation in Serbia which had displayed a total lack of interest in the Serb's in Krajina except in the media, and that is something that lulled the people, as it were. Later on I found out that Milosevic and Franjo Tudjman communicated all the time as they kept this war under control, bearing in mind that they did not want to do anything to destabilise each other, and topple them from their thrones. That has surfaced in the meantime, their joint misdoings concerning money laundering.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You say Dragan threatened the army that he would seek support from the other force within the state. Why was that, in his mind, a threat, if you are able to cast any light on that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because among the people any kind of help given to the Serbs on the other side of the Drina, this led to a surge of good feeling. Soldiers received a salary not only to defend the state, but also the people. As for Croatian secessionism, it had the backing of Germany and the Vatican. Later on we found out that Croatian secessionism --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. So in sum, the DB or the Serbian MUP would become more popular than the military security, and that was the stick Dragan was using against the military to force them to do what he wanted them to do?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The people thought that the military intelligence service recruited its personnel in a stupid way. I'll explain why. The entire civil war could have been done and over with, or rather, prevented altogether through an operation of the military intelligence service in Ljubljana and Zagreb, and for this they had the support of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, can you just try to crystallise what you are trying to say in relation to Dragan and the threat. Just crystallise it in two to three sentences. We know you know a lot but we are interested in this.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were in charge of security and the army would have lost their jobs under the pressure coming from public opinion. Milosevic was popular in Serbia and any failure of the military intelligence services and the military as such would be held against him. In this way, he would have reduced his chances at some future elections. So he was careful. He took into account the public opinion as such. All the time Milosevic pretended to help the Serbs in Krajina but it was play acting rather than reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could you just bring it back to Dragan, please.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan took advantage, or rather, tried to take advantage of this rift and he tried to threaten the military officers and he said that he would do away with their reputation by turning to the police, and they were a lesser force compared to the military because they had only short-barreled weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you just repeat your last comment, please.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the police did not have long-barrelled weapons and that it was not a military force that could participate in a war, as opposed to the army which, through the support of the United States of America, after the conflict with Stalin, became one of the best armies in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The pleasure is mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Weber, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is at the other side of the courtroom and he is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Defence counsel to help me in terms of documents. When referred to certain documents I should be given some assistance because I have my number 1, 2, 3, and when Defence counsel says it's number 6 or 7, then perhaps I can refer to it so that I know exactly what it is that I had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take care that there will be no confusion as to documents your attention will be drawn to. Most likely they will be on your screen. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just picking up where the Stanisic Defence was discussing with you, when did Captain Dragan tell you that he was scaring the army with the DB?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the army was afraid of its reputation being put in danger because Captain Dragan --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was a prominent figure. Your Honours, I was listening to the Serbian interpretation and there was a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You repeat your question, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, when did Captain Dragan tell you that he was scaring the army with the DB? I'm asking you for a date.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that exactly. I said that he told me at a later point when the fuss was over, perhaps a fortnight later, and we were not in constant contact. I was engaged in lecturing abroad before the Serbian audience abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, my questions will be pretty precise, if you could please listen to them carefully and respond to what I'm asking. When were you engaging abroad before the Serbian audience? When was that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was from the spring of 1991, May. I gave lectures in Switzerland, Germany, Vienna, Paris -- no, Paris had been earlier, so Switzerland and Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What exactly did Captain Dragan tell you about what he said to the army about the DB?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could we get a complete answer to your last question. You said it was from the spring of 1991, May. How long were you abroad? Until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went and came back. I would give a lecture or two, spend a week abroad and then return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this continued until when approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It continued until 1992 when I could no longer go abroad because the army proclaimed that if anyone wanted to leave, they had to report to the army first, and as a persona non grata - I am sorry, this is important - I was afraid to be killed in Vukovar because it seemed that all those who were unfit were sent to Vukovar where many died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was seeking clarification in terms of time. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall what Captain Dragan exactly said about his conversations with the army and what he said about the DB? Do you recall what he said?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he used some nasty words, it seems. He told me he had said some of it to the soldiers and that he threatened them with the police. He said they were unpleasantly surprised with how openly he confronted them and he believed them to be softies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: He believed the army to be softies?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers, not the army as such. The officers who were in charge of making decisions. The top brass of the Yugoslav Army. I have to say, though, that there were people of different ethnicities, it wasn't a Serbian army but a Yugoslav one, and he thought that Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, thank you. And I'll move on. How many times did you go to the Krajina with Captain Dragan between January and April 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once. Before that I had gone there alone without Captain Dragan, with Prica and Pavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please focus on my questions and this will go very quickly. The reports provided by the Defence do not indicate that you had any contact with Captain Dragan prior to the end of December 1990. Do you recall precisely when you first met Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the elections which took place in December. I think it must have been in the latter part of October or November 1990. It's been 20 years, you see, and when so many events are occurring in such a short period of time, one quickly loses track and forgets within a month or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How many times did you speak with Captain Dragan during the fall of 1990?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. Numerous times. We socialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can you give an approximation of how frequent?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I socialised more with Prica and Pavic than with my own wife. It was a political struggle. The first parliamentary elections in which we were hoping to topple Milosevic. We were in the offices of the political party from dusk until late at night. We gave speeches and were doing something constantly. It was a historic moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please focus on my questions. I asked you can you give an approximation of how many frequent you interacted or spoke with Captain Dragan during the fall of 1990. I do not see in your answer -- except for the reference that you socialised more with Prica and Pavic than my own wife. Approximately how frequently did you socialise or interact with Captain Dragan during the fall of 1990?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we interacted daily, basically, unless he was away on his trips.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Great. On page 43 of yesterday's transcript, you were asked the question: "In the beginning of 1991, did Daniel Snedden travel somewhere?" You were asked this question on two occasions on yesterday's transcript. The first time you responded that he, referring to Daniel Snedden, and Pavic went to Thessaloniki unannounced. The second time you were asked this question, you stated that Captain Dragan went to the United States on your instructions. Is it correct that you are describing two different trips?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two different trips. One to Solun and the other --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be more precise: He didn't go to the US on my instruction, he went there on his own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you can please focus on my questions, and again yes, no if it calls for it, or I don't know. Which one of these trips happened first?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he went to the US first.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How much time was there between the two trips?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did he travel to Greece and for how long?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stayed for a few days until the weather improved and Pavic came shortly afterwards the next day or thereabout by train.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On how many occasions did Captain Dragan travel to the United States between January and April 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did he travel to the United States, and for how long?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You have no idea what month this occurred or for what duration, whether it be a day or three weeks that he was gone while you were in contact with him on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you focus more on my answers, please focus on what I'm saying. I was in standing contact with him at the time of the elections in 1990. In 1991 we were no longer in daily contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pleasure is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 44 of yesterday's transcript, you discussed the establishment of a new political party, the Serbian Democratic Union. You stated that: "Our contact person was supposed to be Daniel Snedden because he had the opportunity to travel and establish contacts in an unhindered way in the United States of America." Is it correct that you left the SPO before Captain Dragan travelled to the United States?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the SPO in early January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this before Captain Dragan travelled to the United States?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 38 of yesterday's transcript you stated: "Captain Dragan communicated with Vuk Draskovic and the latter's political team. According to his estimate he defined them as soft, as soft people who were not up to the political situation at hand and the demands that were ahead of us." On page 45 you were asked about the contents of your Serbian DB report that stated: "We can conclude that he is basically dissatisfied with the positions of the SPO because he," referring to Captain Dragan, "says that the leadership of that party are a group of soft people who don't know what they want." When did you hear Captain Dragan call the leadership of the SPO soft?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a general view. It doesn't necessarily mean that he uttered it and then I remembered it. It was my view as well and Pavic's and Prica's. We thought they were not up to the task and it was almost a mantra of sorts. They didn't seem to be up to the requirements of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, lines 16 and 17, the witness added another name which is not reflected in the transcript. Perhaps we can clarify with the witness as to whose opinion it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pavic, Prica, I had the same view as well as many others, including Daniel Snedden. It was a mantra of sorts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any independent recollection of Daniel Snedden, Captain Dragan, saying that the SPO leadership was soft? Him actually having a conversation with you about that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked constantly, even before the elections. Our position had been crystallised before the elections in December so it was in October and November of 1990. Serbia at the time needed a statesman, not a politician; whereas, Vuk Draskovic was merely a good politician and/orator.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is that a yes, that you do have a recollection of Captain Dragan telling you this?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are suggesting an answer which is not very nice, sir. I cannot say recalling that at this or that time by raising his eyebrow Captain Dragan said this or that thing. It was a general view. We were in consensus and we repeated it often all of us, and it would be strange for me to remember any single such occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked whether you discussed it during your conversations, whether you have a recollection of that, and then you started answering that you talked constantly, which is not a very direct answer. So do I understand that in your conversations with Daniel Snedden, he at least once, if not more times, said that the SPO leadership was soft? Is that how I have to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And let's try not to comment on the questions put to you and how nice it is. If you have any problem, address me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in line 24, there is no answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that the witness seemed to agree with my suggestion that if that would be any problem -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, he nodded and apparently said something but in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think he said -- well, he agreed, let's move on and Mr. Weber, you are the first one to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 55 of yesterday's transcript, you stated: "We went there, actually this telephone contact was in January, if I can remember correctly. And then with --"

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Captain Dragan and myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, let me finish my question, please. Your quote was: "We went there, actually this telephone contact was in January, if I remember correctly. And then with Pavic and Prica we went to the Knin Krajina and we met some people with the political structures there. As far as I can remember, Zdravkovic was there. The president of the municipality of Benkovac." Mr. Bakrac then corrected you and suggested that this person's name is Zecevic. Do you recall the first name of the president of the municipality of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember his first name is Zdravko, that's why I said Zdravkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What month did you have this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You stated that: "We met some people with the political structures there." Who else did you meet with and where did this meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held at the monastery on the Krka waterfalls. I forgot what the name of the monastery is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who was present at this meeting besides yourself, Pavic, and Prica?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another man from the security service, and I think there was someone there from the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was the person from the security service Dusan Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know Dusan Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who was this other man from the security service?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a tall man. I think he was a policeman with the Croatian MUP. A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. He was unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you say that because this individual did not say much during your meeting?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Between January and April 1991, how many phone conversations did you have with Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would you say that you were in regular phone contact with him?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Serbia. I did say that I went abroad to lecture. Up to what date or between what dates, January and?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you between January and April 1991, and if I understand correctly, you said that from May 1991 you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, Mr. Simatovic is a personal friend of yours; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is not a personal friend. He is a classmate but I have many classmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how often did you see Franko Simatovic between 1989 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We lived on the same street. My father and daughter were in Svetozar Markovic Street and I lived nearby. I frequently came to his street and would meet him once or twice a year or so, and then we would just sit down, have a drink, or wave at each other in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how often did you talk with Franko Simatovic by telephone between 1989 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any telephone conversations with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic is also a personal friend of yours; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with some other 600 classmates, colleagues from the school of journalism. In our terms, a friend is someone who comes to your patron saints celebration, but he never attended any of mine or I of his, especially in view the fact that he doesn't celebrate his patron saints day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You also knew Jovica Stanisic between 1989 and 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him back from the university but we also knew Franjo Tudjman's son because we happened to have attended the same elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a moment. Did you know that Franko Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic were employed by the Serbian State Security Service prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know that. Before 1991, yes, I knew, and everyone else in Belgrade knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you saying that everyone else in Belgrade knew that -- who Franko Simatovic was and that he was a member of the Serbian DB prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you are right. Well, it wasn't that widely known before 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you claim that this past Monday was the first time you learned the Serbian DB conducted operative processing on you between 1989 and April 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I learned about it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in all of the reports that you were shown by the Defence that none of your contacts with Mr. Simatovic or Mr. Stanisic were reflected in those documents?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I apologise for asking you a negative and then you responding with a negative, so if we could just -- as I understand your answer, the reports do not contain any references to your contacts with the accused, do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. When I met with Franko I discussed what I was writing at the time. I was writing Pavlovic's testimony -- testament at the time, and since he was a communist, I was trying to indoctrinate him of sorts with my ideas of anti-communism because I believe it to be the opium for the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, there seems to be a confusion. What Mr. Weber asked you is whether the documents that were shown to you by the Defence, whether those documents do not contain any reference to your contacts with the accused. So not about whether you had any contacts with the accused, but whether that's reflected in any of the documents shown to you by the Defence. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could see that I was subjected to DB treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which is not a direct reference to contact with Mr. Simatovic or Mr. Stanisic, but rather with the DB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any -- please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did Franko Simatovic ever tell you that he authorised the monitoring of your telephone while you were having conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not conduct any conversations with him, as I've already said, and he did not tell me that he was monitoring my telephone calls, as you had put it. We never discussed that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did either Franko Simatovic or Jovica Stanisic discuss their work with you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you speak more directly into the microphone. The interpreters have difficulties hearing you. So could you then repeat your answer to the question, whether either Franko Simatovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or Jovica Stanisic discussed their work with you. The answer is no. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In 1991 did either Franko Simatovic or Jovica Stanisic discuss their interactions with Captain Dragan with you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know Dragan Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I met him once when we sat at this tavern called Mala Madera [phoen] together with Franko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I know the weather was nice. I know that we were sitting outdoors. I can't remember exactly when it happened. It was the spring of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recall how Dragan Filipovic introduced himself to you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that his nickname was Fica and he said that he was Franko's assistant or associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It was your understanding based on that introduction that Fica was a subordinate of Mr. Simatovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: From this interaction that you had with Fica, did you realise that Fica knew a lot about you?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: From the reports that the Defence showed you, did you learn that it was Dragan Filipovic who was the one that was conducting the monitoring of you between December and April -- December 1990 and April 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that from the signatures in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever work with Franko Simatovic or Jovica Stanisic or for them?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you ever been an official source or associate of the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you ever received any payments from the Serbian DB, whether it be for salary, per diems, or monetary compensation for any information?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you ever made any payments to a member of the Serbian DB for information?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As a journalist, did you ever see any media reports that mentioned either Mr. Simatovic or Mr. Stanisic prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have publicly relied on your friendships with the accused to sell your books over the past 17 years?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Marketing, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Aside from your four fiction novels, have you always published what you know to be the truth or have you published what can be considered propaganda?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are four novels and the rest are non-fiction and historiography that apply the method of quotation from other books and from the Internet and this involves footnotes with proper references.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Am I to understand correctly that aside from your four fiction novels that you are asserting that what you published to be the truth?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I'm trying to say that it's the truth. In addition to these books with quotes, there were other books that are in the field of investigative journalism, that is to say investigating crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6329 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, do you recognise this interview dated 23 December 2009 which is posted on your website www.dejanlucic.net?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this interview related to a book that you published entitled: "The Conspiracy Theory," which, according to you, is "a manual as to how to create your own secret society, how to infiltrate political parties, conquer them from within, and become a new caliph in the place of the existing one." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The word caliph, is that a reference to a head of state of an Islamic community or empire?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of the English translation and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, during this interview you were asked: "Do you have reliable sources? Who is assisting you?" Your answer: "Some people think that police has nothing better to do than provide information for writers! Do you really think that there is anyone within the secret service who knows what I'm writing about?! Do I know some intelligence officers? Of course. Frenki Simatovic is my classmate. I know him for 52 years. Jovica Stanisic is also a friend of mine. We studied political science together. I also went to school with Miroslav Tudjman, who is very wise man, but his father attacked me in his book "Polovina raspuca."

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Historical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just not to confuse the witness, the interpretation was that Franko Simatovic was a colleague of his, whereas I see that the original says "schoolmate," "classmate." I'm just trying to prevent any kind of confusion. The interpretation the witness received said "colleague" rather than "schoolmate" or "classmate."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least that is your recollection. We could verify that whether it was translated to the witness as colleague where the original doesn't say "classmate." The original -- well, the original translation says "classmate" which, of course, is not yet the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour the original is correct. The written translation is correct. The interpretation he received in his headphones was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, we usually verify with the interpreters what is right and what is wrong, but if it was translated as "colleague" then that may have created some confusion if "classmate" would be the right -- would be the right translation. Could I hear from the B/C/S booth, and I have then to switch to 6. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also need to add something for the sake of history. The book written by Franjo Tudjman was not called "Polovina" as it says here, but "Povjesna raspuca." So it was a crossroads of history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to get back to where we were. Mr. Weber read a portion of this interview to you. I think he made a small mistake in quoting the question, which was not "do you have reliable sources," but "do you have reliable police sources" who is assisting you. I think now we have a perfect view on what it says here, and now Mr. Weber is going to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Simatovic, Mr. Stanisic, or Franjo Tudjman's son Miroslav a source for your book entitled "The Conspiracy Theory"?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not. I was not no contact with them in relation to that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have known Mr. Simatovic since you were both nine years old?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. We have known each other since the time we were both seven years old. We went together to elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting my math. Slobodan Rajh is a kum or best man of Franko Simatovic; correct? Rajh spelled R-a-j-h.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see here is the English -- what does it say here, thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, there's no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Rajh -- what is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need to read the transcript. It's important that you answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether Slobodan Rajh is a kum or best man for Simatovic. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether he is his kum. I don't know what kind of relationship the two of them have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have known Mr. Stanisic since he attended school of political science in Belgrade in the early 1970s?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you last talk to Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you last talk to Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2008 I think it was, at his home. I took him a book as a present, and then he asked me, "Lucic, where did you get all that information?" I laughed and said, "Don't ask me, everybody has been saying that you've been providing me with this information." The trick is that the book is full of all kinds of information that is history based, and the police cannot help me with that because they do not deal with history.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've also been saying that they've been providing you with information; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. I said that by way of a joke. And when I took him the book and he asked me where did you get all this information, and I laughed, smiled, said why are you asking because everybody has been saying that you've been providing me with information. The book is full of quotations, and I know exactly which quotation comes from which book. In the Serbian language or from newspaper articles, this is the history of Khazars for instance, from the mid-8th century until the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The Prosecution at this time tenders 6329 into evidence, the article before the Chamber, as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6329 will receive number P3053, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6336.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is going to be appearing an article in interview from 25 November 1994 entitled: "Mysteries of Everyday Life. The Rise of Dejan Lucic. The Elite in the Underworld." Did you provide this interview in 1994?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which newspaper is this that carried this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It was "Intervju"?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is the author? Who is the author?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Lucic, one, I take it that Mr. Weber is considering whether he can find the author. There's no need to repeat that question, yet. Mr. Weber, do you have the name of an author or is it without?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Offhand, I do not see it on this first page. I can further check. We might have information about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you, though: This purports to be an interview with you containing your statements. So even without knowing the author, do you recall providing this interview in 1994?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This interview quotes you as saying: "Now that people have given me that opportunity, I enjoy playing with this image." Do you recall making that statement, and if so, what people are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before we continue, at the end of this interview a name appears which is Vojislav Tufekcic.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aha, Vojislav Tufekcic. Now I remember the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then perhaps you resume, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lucic, do you now recall providing this interview?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the interview, you stated: "Now that people have given me that opportunity, I enjoy playing with this image." What people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who am I referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interview was given in 1994 when my book was published. Since Vuk Draskovic, after he lost the election in 1990, launched a story to the effect that I was a spy, then I thought that it could not be helped, I could not get rid of this label that was placed on me. It's just like when somebody is said to be gay, the more he keeps saying that he is not, the more everybody is convinced that he is in a Christian environment. So I turned this into a marketing trick and I wrote a book in the field of espionage. In his book called "Target" that was written by Vuk Draskovic, who is part of the government to this day, he wrote that I was a secret service agent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again there is a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you would like to verify the translation. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness kindly repeat what Mr. Lucic said; what did Vuk Draskovic accuse him of? For which secret service was he working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vuk Draskovic in his book "The Target," and he has a wife who is the main intelligence person within the political party, he wrote this book, published in a huge number of copies, about two years ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not seeking additional answers. We are just seeking to verify whether the translation was accurate and complete. You said: "He wrote that I was a secret service agent." Was there anything more you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military secret service agent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of the B/C/S and page -- B/C/S, actually, and English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the far left column, four paragraphs from the top of this page. This article states in part: "Regarding speculations that he wrote the secrets of the Albanian Mafia with the help of his next door neighbour Jovica Stanisic, head of the Republic's Security Service, he says with apparent calm, 'Jovica Stanisic is our and their colleague. If I am to be blamed for knowing a lot of people, I can live with that.'" Was Jovica Stanisic also your neighbour, and if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was my neighbour at Banjica, and our children went to elementary school together for I don't know how long exactly. I cannot remember now. I was there until 1990 for a year, for a few years. I don't know when Jovica was given another apartment and when he moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Please let me know if I have it correct. You were neighbours prior to 1990 then for a few years?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I moved to that apartment in Banjica during my first marriage in 1983 and I lived there until 1990 until I got divorced. Then Jovica Stanisic lived in the next door building, and as a child I lived in the street Svetozar Markovica [phoen] and my neighbours were Franko Simatovic and Miroslav Tudjman. These are different periods of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. This passage refers to speculation that you wrote your book with the help of Jovica Stanisic. That book being "The Secrets of the Albanian Mafia." When did this speculation occur?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these speculations were voiced after 1991, I think, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic help you write your book, "The Secrets of the Albanian Mafia."

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked for help -- actually, I didn't ask him. I didn't even know that he worked for state security. I went to see Mitrovic who at the time was chief of state security, and during that meeting with Mitrovic, Jovica Stanisic appeared, and I mean, I was surprised but that was in 1988, that's when the book was published. And Jovica Stanisic, well, this was 1983, at the time, I mean, I did not even know -- 1983, 1983. That's when I moved to Banjica, and this was in 1988 -- I mean, the book was published in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you learn that Jovica Stanisic worked for the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I came to see Mitrovic to collect material for that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That book was being created for a number of years. First it was published as a phaton [phoen] in "Novosti," then in "Ekspres Politika," and only then it was published as a book. And let me remember, I think it was sometime in 1985, 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have the next section of this article that is lower in bold. It's the section entitled: "The Man Who Brought Captain Dragan to Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first try to find out, you said you learned that Jovica Stanisic worked for the State Security Service, and when was that, and you say in -- oh, that was in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1985, 1986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I see that it's 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Lucic. I wanted to turn your attention back to the article that we were discussing from "Intervju" in 1994 in the section entitled: "The Man Who Brought Captain Dragan to Serbia." You were quoted in this section as saying that Captain Dragan: "... first went to Draskovic's HQ but there they completely ignored him, then he came to me." Is it correct that Captain Dragan was ignored by the SPO in late 1990 and early 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to understand that Daniel Snedden at the time was one of hundreds of people arriving from the rest of the world at the SPO. It was a magnet basically for all former emigres and anti-communists. At the time Daniel Snedden appeared, among other people, there were many others who were coming from abroad with money in their bags in order to finance the SPO and assisting to topple the regime. In such circumstances, you will understand that Daniel Snedden could not attract much attention by those who were in charge of the party. He came to see and he noticed that many people went through my office but we were still hungry most of the time, and he asked whether we had enough money. I told him we had enough money to eat but for ourselves, but he didn't -- we didn't have enough money to feed everyone else. Then he proposed that we -- this is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Weber interrupts you, he is entitled to do so if you move rather --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- far away from what the question was. If there's anything at the very end of your testimony which you consider of such importance that you should convey it to us, you'll have an opportunity to do so. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a very simple question, yes or no. Do you stand by your 1994 statement that Captain Dragan was completely ignored by the SPO?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say he was completely ignored. I just said that he didn't receive much attention. It doesn't mean that they ceased any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you then say "then he came to me," is it correct that this is a reference to your initial contact with Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This article states: "Lucic's political career ended ingloriously when he was suspected within his own party of scheming with the State Security Service, SDB. Accusations by his idealogical comrades in arms were very rough and they included embezzlement. When the accusations were still fresh, he decided not to dispute them in public." Is this statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When exactly did your own party, which I'm understanding this to be the SPO, consider you as scheming with the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. The stories of me being a secret agent of the SDB were launched by Zvonimir Trajkovic, one of Slobodan Milosevic's advisors because my organisation, the Belgrade board, represented a greater danger for the regime than the SPO itself all over Serbia. This proved correct during elections because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can focus you in, my question goes to when. By your answer, is it correct that this occurred at the end of 1990, this speculation?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is there any truth to the speculation? Were you cooperating with the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was trying to explain a moment ago as to who initiated such rumours and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, it's understood. Is it correct that you have not done anything to dissuade or refute the speculation about your relationship with the accused or the Serbian DB over the past 20 years?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't do that. I couldn't refute something that is impossible to refute. How can you deny something that doesn't exist in the first place? Do not forget that Vuk Draskovic participated in power at the time of Slobodan Milosevic as he is doing nowadays as well, and I'm just another writer or journalist. His voice against me carried much greater weight than anything I would have to say against him. It would be like tearing a pillow up on the 20th floor and trying to make someone pick up all the feathers down on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have done nothing to dissuade or refute the speculation about your relationship with the accused and the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's the same question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said I couldn't do that. That seems to imply that what you couldn't do you didn't do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an answer to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have any criminal complaints ever been filed against you in relation to the publication of any of your books?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they have, by a municipality which was dissatisfied with my view of history expressed in one of my books -- no, sorry, there were two complaints; one by Alija Izetbegovic, the leader of the Muslim immigration community in Zurich in Switzerland about the book "The Secrets of the Albanian Mafia"; the second suit or complaint concerned a partisan official concerning Pavelic's crimes and the crimes of communists against Serbs in Montenegro. I was brought before a court but was not pronounced guilty in either of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. With respect to the second complaint, is that in relation to either of your books "The Kingdom of the Khazars" or "The Kingdom of the Khazars 2"?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the third book. I think the book in question is "The Kingdom of the Khazars 2," but it never reached the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you are referring to Khazars, who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A people. Arthur Koestler described them in his book.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the name of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They live between the Caspian Sea and the Black Sea, and they accepted Judaism in the middle ages. These are mainly the Ashkenazi Jews nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please provide a very brief description about what you write about the Jews in your books "The Kingdom of the Khazars" and "The Kingdom of the Khazars 2"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wonder why this is relevant, these questions about books and the history of the Khazars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's relevant to the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Credibility of the witness is apparently the -- let's see where we get to. I do not know -- do you know the book, Mr. -- let's -- I'll give Mr. Weber an opportunity to further develop his line of questioning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please provide a brief description about what you write about the Jews in your books "The Kingdom of the Khazars" and "The Kingdom of the Khazars 2"?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to correct the Prosecutor. These are not Jews but the Khazars and it's titled as such. His obvious attempt to paint me as a person of anti-Semitic sentiments is ludicrous because I have great respect for the values of the Jewish people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are the books about?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the history of the Khazars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll leave it there for the time being and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6339.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, the Simatovic Defence noticed a large number of reports from the Serbian DB and primarily showed you documents from December 1990 to the beginning of April 1991. The Prosecution would like to focus with you on some specific information in these reports between the dates of July 1990 and April 1991. We have prepared a demonstrative time-line for the purpose of discussing this information with you. The chart is now before you on the screen. Directing your attention to the first entry for 12 July 1990. From your testimony here today, do I understand correctly that you did not know Captain Dragan when he first arrived to Belgrade? Sir, if you could please focus on the chart that's before you and not the chart with your comments. Sir, my question to you was, do I understand correctly that you did not know Captain Dragan when he first arrived to Belgrade on the 12th of July, 1990?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to the information in the possession of the Serbian DB, Captain Dragan made a total of 14 flights between 12 July and 14 December, 1990. Did you know that Captain Dragan was making these frequent flights?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next entry for September to December 1990. According to you today, you've indicated that you met Captain Dragan around the time of the election in 1990. When after that did you learn of his business and his residence with Branka Popovic?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branka Popovic, a female. Let me tell you, his private affairs were of no interest to me at the time of the elections. I hardly had any time for my own private affairs. And I don't even remember meeting Daniel and his girlfriend in that period before December. Perhaps I met her later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next entry for 10 and 11 December, 1990. Could you please read this entry and let the Chamber know when you need the next page.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, have you finished reading the entry?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you know that Captain Dragan had three different passports?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I only saw the Australian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did Captain Dragan initially introduce himself to you as Daniel Snedden?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you first learn that Captain Dragan's real name was Dragan Vasiljkovic and not Daniel Snedden?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he said so on RTL, the TV station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was that in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. In any case, the broadcast was on RTL.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you first hear him called Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already. I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What I'm asking is the phrase "Captain Dragan," did you hear that during the same broadcast on RTL?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said as much. We all knew him as Daniel, we were completely unaware of Dragan or Captain Dragan. We called him Daniel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I intentionally delayed my interruption to -- for you to be able to see whether this is of any help, but the Prosecution actually uses the name of Daniel Snedden in many documents and reports they have, and yet they discuss Captain Dragan with the witness. I think enough was asked of the witness and this is all unfair. If they want to put a document to him, it's fine. I'm just looking at the tables drafted by the Prosecutor. There are references to Captain Dragan and Daniel Snedden which may cause some confusion. I delayed my intervention, and in the mean time we were able to hear the answers of the witness and he clarified the situation. In any case, it is unfair that the Prosecution uses this strategy in their table. It is against the rules of cross-examination. They can put suggestive questions, leading questions, but I don't think this is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which rule of cross-examination, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correctly presenting documents to a witness. All documents the Prosecution refers to mentions Daniel Snedden in the original and in their table they introduce Captain Dragan which may cause confusion and lead the witness to a wrong track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not know. So if I understand you well, is that the table used by the Prosecution does not reflect what is said but replaces the name -- the one name by the other, is that your concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to intervene in that respect, and their other references to documents were correct. Simply put, in all of the documents we have Daniel Snedden, not Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was answered by the yes, because I wanted to give an opportunity to Mr. Weber to say something about it. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first it's cross-examination and the Prosecution is using a demonstrative exhibit to put something to the witness. With respect to the individual that we are talking about, I think it's pretty clear that the same individual is Captain Dragan, Daniel Snedden, Dragan Vasiljkovic. The documents that Mr. Bakrac is referring to between December 1990 and April 1991 do refer to this individual Captain Dragan, Dragan Vasiljkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- as Daniel Snedden, so I'm putting to the witness a demonstrative exhibit. It does say Captain Dragan. We do acknowledge that the documents reflect Daniel Snedden during this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think it would have been best in a table where you are still seeking the comment of the witness on, isn't it, that you use name used in the document and that you can verify whether it's the same person, either in one question for all of the documents or for each document. That seems to be the best approach. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And we will do so, Your Honour, in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Skipping to the entry for 24 December 1991, could you please review this entry and let us know when you are done.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The 24th of December.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know why Pavic told Captain Dragan to turn to you and Radomir Zivkovic when his plane was grounded?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told him to get in touch with me since Pavic, Prica, and Daniel were in a way foreigners in Belgrade and didn't know people. That is why they turned to me as the oldest among them to try and resolve a problem. So he suggested to Daniel Snedden to turn to me, and I forwarded him to Radomir Zivkovic because he obviously had some legal issues with the state. A person best placed to deal with such was our party lawyer from our Belgrade board.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did Captain Dragan ever tell you that he was aware of individuals listening to his telephone after 24 December 1990?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, we did think that we were being tapped. In the system as existed then, as it is the case in Serbia now, it is basically part of folklore. However, we couldn't use pigeons, so we relied on telephones despite our fears. I don't remember, though, that his phone was being tapped at the time. I see here that he made a remark to those eavesdropping that he was not a terrorist. Well, I can say that he certainly was not a terrorist, and when I saw him being described as a terrorist and someone inciting to terrorism is an exaggeration. I don't know what the reasons were for the police to wire-tap him and monitor him, perhaps to earn their wages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll be directing your attention to the entry for 9 January 1991. My question to you will be, when did you first learn that there was contact between Milan Ostojic and Daniel Snedden?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN LUCIC [Resumed]
